title: Who regulates you
body: The Nevada Real Estate Division licenses and investigates. It sits in the Department of Business and Industry and is run by the Administrator. The Real Estate Commission, appointed by the Governor, adopts regulations and decides discipline.
example: A Henderson agent renews online with the Division; a complaint against them goes before the Commission.
hook: The Division runs it. The Commission rules on it.

title: Statutes and regulations
body: NRS 645 is the license law passed by the Legislature. NAC 645 holds the regulations adopted under it. Both bind every Nevada licensee, and the Division investigates violations of either.
example: Advertising rules for brokerage names come from NAC 645; the duties owed to clients come from NRS 645.
hook: NRS is the law. NAC fills in the details.

title: From complaint to hearing
body: Anyone can file a complaint with the Division. The Division investigates, and if it finds a likely violation, the case can go to a Commission hearing. The licensee can respond and present evidence.
example: A Reno buyer files a complaint about missing earnest money. The Division audits the broker's trust records.
hook: Complaint, investigation, hearing, decision.

title: Penalties
body: The Commission can reprimand, require education, place conditions, suspend or revoke a license, and fine up to $10,000 per violation. A licensee can seek judicial review of the final decision in district court.
example: A Las Vegas licensee who commingled funds is fined and ordered to take a trust account course.
hook: Up to $10,000 per violation.

title: The Recovery Fund
body: The Education, Research and Recovery Fund pays people who won a court judgment against a licensee for fraud, misrepresentation, or deceit in a transaction and couldn't collect it. Payouts have per-judgment and per-licensee limits.
example: A Henderson seller wins a fraud judgment against a licensee who has no assets and applies to the Fund.
hook: Win in court first, then apply to the Fund.

title: When the Fund pays
body: Commonly cited limits are $25,000 per judgment and $100,000 for all claims involving one licensee. When the Fund pays, the licensee's license is suspended until they repay the Fund with interest.
example: After the Fund pays a claim, the Reno licensee can't practice until they repay it.
hook: The Fund pays; the licensee pays it back.

title: Who needs a license
body: Anyone who, for compensation, sells, buys, lists, exchanges, leases, or negotiates real estate for someone else needs a Nevada license. An unlicensed person can't sue to collect a commission.
example: A Las Vegas friend who "helps" a neighbor sell for a fee is acting illegally without a license.
hook: For others, for pay? Get licensed.

title: Common exemptions
body: Owners selling their own property don't need a license. Neither do people acting under court order, like an executor or receiver, in that role. Exemptions are narrow; check the statute before relying on one.
example: A Carson City owner sells their own home without an agent. No license needed.
hook: Your own property, no license needed.

title: Three licenses
body: A salesperson works only under a broker. A broker-salesperson holds broker qualifications but works under another broker. A broker can run a brokerage and supervise others.
example: An experienced Reno agent passes the broker exam but stays at her firm as a broker-salesperson.
hook: Salesperson under, broker over.

title: Permits on top of a license
body: Some specialties need a permit added to the license. Property management requires a property management permit. Acting as a business broker requires a business broker permit.
example: A Las Vegas salesperson who wants to manage rentals for owners must first get a property management permit.
hook: Managing rentals? Get the permit.

title: Getting licensed
body: Complete pre-licensing education at an NRED-approved school, register and pay through NRED, pass both exam portions, submit fingerprints for a background check, and apply with a sponsoring broker. Check the Roadmap for current amounts.
example: A Henderson student finishes school, passes both portions, then files the application with fingerprints and a broker.
hook: School, exam, prints, broker, application.

title: Honesty on the application
body: The Division reviews background checks and applicants' honesty. Failing to disclose a past conviction or license discipline on the application can itself be grounds for denial.
example: A Reno applicant discloses an old misdemeanor up front with court documents.
hook: Disclose it before they find it.

title: Keeping your license
body: New licensees complete post-licensing education in their first year. After that, licenses renew on a cycle with continuing education, including required topics like agency, contracts, ethics, and law. Miss CE and you can't renew active.
example: A Las Vegas agent finishes her CE a month early so her renewal isn't delayed.
hook: First year: post-licensing. Every cycle: CE.

title: Active, inactive, and moving
body: A salesperson must be associated with a broker to be active. If the association ends, the license becomes inactive and the licensee can't practice until they associate with a new broker through the Division.
example: A Henderson salesperson leaves one firm on Friday and can't show homes until the new association is processed.
hook: No broker, no business.

title: The broker's responsibility
body: A Nevada broker must supervise the salespeople and broker-salespeople associated with them, including their transactions, advertising, and handling of money. Licensees may be paid only through their broker.
example: A Reno broker reviews new agents' contracts before they go out.
hook: The broker answers for the team.

title: Pay and personal deals
body: Salespeople can't accept compensation from anyone but their broker, and can't pay unlicensed people for licensed work. When dealing for themselves, licensees must disclose their license status.
example: A Las Vegas agent buying a rental for herself tells the seller in writing that she's licensed.
hook: All pay through the broker; license status out loud.

title: Trust money in Nevada
body: Money received for others must be deposited as NRS 645.310 requires, usually in the broker's trust account or with escrow. Commingling and conversion are grounds for discipline. Brokers keep records the Division may inspect and audit.
example: A Henderson broker deposits earnest money directly with the escrow company named in the contract.
hook: Deposit it right, record it all.

title: Keep the records
body: Brokers must keep transaction and trust records for the period Nevada law requires and make them available to the Division. Missing records can count as a violation.
example: During an audit, a Las Vegas broker produces every deposit slip and ledger in minutes.
hook: If it isn't recorded, it didn't happen.

title: Advertising in Nevada
body: Ads must include the brokerage's licensed name and must not be false or misleading. Team and personal ads still need the brokerage. Licensees advertising their own property must disclose that they're licensed.
example: A Reno team's yard sign shows the team name and, as required, the brokerage name.
hook: Always show the brokerage.

title: Online and social media
body: Websites, social posts, and texts are advertising. The same rules apply: identify the brokerage, be accurate, and don't advertise listings without permission.
example: A Las Vegas agent's Instagram bio includes the brokerage name.
hook: Any medium, same rules.

title: Prohibited acts
body: Nevada law lists grounds for discipline, including misrepresentation, false promises, commingling, failing to account for money, acting for more than one party without written consent, and paying unlicensed people for licensed work.
example: A Henderson agent promises a buyer the home will double in value in two years. That's a false promise.
hook: Lie, mix, hide, or pay the unlicensed: discipline.

title: Conduct beyond transactions
body: Certain criminal convictions, unpaid child support orders, and dishonest conduct generally can also lead to discipline. Licensees must cooperate with Division investigations.
example: A Reno licensee who ignores the Division's request for records can be disciplined for that alone.
hook: Cooperate with the Division.
